honesty: Each record cites a real source. Unknown fields are 'UNKNOWN', never invented. Vitality reflects the cited authority's classification. ISO 15924 codes were verified against the Unicode ISO 15924 Registration Authority four-letter code table (iso15924-codes.html). Provenance URLs were actually retrieved or surfaced via web search during research on 2026-06-16.

sources.name: Atlas of Endangered Alphabets (Endangered Alphabets Project, Tim Brookes)
ISO 15924 Registration Authority (Unicode) - four-letter code table
Omniglot - the online encyclopedia of writing systems
UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger (classifications cited by secondary sources)

scripts.name: Avestan
scripts.region: Historical Sasanian Persia; Zoroastrian liturgical use today
scripts.vitalityBasis: Created by Sasanian scribes (3rd-7th c. CE) to record the Avesta; the Avestan language ceased as a vernacular ~400 BCE and the script survives only as a Zoroastrian liturgical script

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Avestan
Sasanian-era script; liturgical use; Unicode block U+10B00-10B3F; ISO 15924 Avst (134)

scripts.name: Balinese
scripts.vitalityBasis: Brahmic abugida for Balinese; everyday literacy is limited and largely displaced by Latin script, though taught and used ceremonially with ongoing revitalization

provenance.note: Brahmic abugida from Kawi; declining everyday use; ISO 15924 Bali (360); block U+1B00-1B7F
ScriptSource Balinese record

scripts.name: Buhid
scripts.vitalityBasis: One of the surviving Philippine Brahmic scripts, still used by the Buhid Mangyan but by a small and declining community

provenance.note: Philippine Brahmic abugida; surviving indigenous script of the Buhid Mangyan; ISO 15924 Buhd (372); block U+1740-175F
ScriptSource Buhid record

scripts.name: Chakma (Ajhā pāṭh)
scripts.region: Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh and India
scripts.vitalityBasis: Classified Definitely Endangered by the UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger (per Endangered Alphabets); few Chakma can still read their own script

provenance.note: Atlas entry: classified Definitely Endangered by UNESCO Atlas; few can still read the script
Brahmic abugida from Burmese/Pallava; Unicode 6.1

scripts.name: Cherokee
scripts.region: Oklahoma and North Carolina, United States
scripts.vitalityBasis: Cherokee language classified by UNESCO as Definitely Endangered (Oklahoma) / Severely Endangered (North Carolina); state of emergency declared 2019, with active immersion-school revitalization

provenance.note: Invented by Sequoyah ~1820s; UNESCO definitely/severely endangered; Tri-Council state of emergency 2019; ISO 15924 Cher (445); blocks U+13A0-13FF and U+AB70-ABBF

scripts.name: Hanunó'o
scripts.vitalityBasis: Philippine Brahmic script still actively used by the Hanunó'o Mangyan, notably for love poetry (ambahan), but by a small indigenous community

provenance.note: Philippine Brahmic abugida; used by Hanunó'o Mangyan; ISO 15924 Hano (371); block U+1720-173F
ScriptSource Hanunoo record

scripts.name: Kawi (Old Javanese)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Historic Brahmic script used across maritime Southeast Asia c. 8th-16th centuries; no longer in living use, ancestral to several modern Indonesian/Philippine scripts

provenance.note: Historic Brahmic script c. 8th-16th c.; ancestral to modern SE Asian scripts; ISO 15924 Kawi (368); block U+11F00-11F5F
ScriptSource Kawi record

scripts.name: Kharosthi (Kharoshthi)
scripts.region: Gandhara, northwest Indian subcontinent, Central Asia
scripts.vitalityBasis: Ancient right-to-left script used for Gandhari Prakrit, Pali, Saka, and Sanskrit; historical use is attested, but no living everyday community use is certified in this system.

provenance.note: Unicode Kharoshthi chart: range U+10A00-U+10A5F and official character names.
ISO 15924 code list: Khar (305), Kharoshthi.
Secondary overview: ancient RTL script of Gandhara; period 4th century BCE to 3rd century CE; Unicode alias Kharoshthi.

scripts.name: Lepcha (Róng)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Brahmic abugida for Lepcha/Róng; reported as endangered with oral knowledge disappearing, though it is an official language of Sikkim and taught in schools

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Rong/Lepcha
Abugida; published Unicode 5.1 (2008); culture reported endangered (2008)

scripts.name: Limbu (Sirijanga)
scripts.region: Eastern Nepal, Sikkim and northeastern India
scripts.vitalityBasis: Brahmic abugida for the Limbu language (~400,000 speakers); revived in the 1920s but remains a minority script under pressure from Devanagari/Nepali

provenance.note: Brahmic abugida; revival in the 1920s; Unicode U+1900-194F
ScriptSource Limbu record

scripts.name: Manchu
scripts.vitalityBasis: Writes the critically endangered Manchu language; Manchu proper has no known native speakers as of 2024, an imperial script that fell nearly into extinction

provenance.note: Atlas entry: imperial script that fell almost into extinction; adapted from Mongol script 1599
Manchu proper has no known native speakers as of 2024; encoded with Mongolian script in Unicode

scripts.name: Mandaic
scripts.vitalityBasis: Liturgical script of the Mandaean religion; Neo-Mandaic severely endangered with ~200 or fewer first-language speakers, per the Atlas of Endangered Alphabets

provenance.note: Atlas entry: ~5,500 Neo-Mandaic speakers, 200 or fewer first-language speakers, severely reduced by persecution and war
Corroborates Aramaic descent, sacred/liturgical status

scripts.name: Mayan Hieroglyphs
scripts.vitalityBasis: Logosyllabic script of the Maya civilization; active use ended after the Spanish conquest, with no continuous community of users since

provenance.note: ISO 15924 code Maya (090) is registered; the script is not yet encoded in Unicode (no allocated block)
Logosyllabic Maya script; use ended after Spanish conquest; ISO 15924 Maya; not yet in Unicode

scripts.name: Mende Kikakui
scripts.vitalityBasis: Pushed into the background by the colonial-era adoption of Latin-based Africa Alphabet in the 1930s; still used today by an estimated few hundred individuals, with recent revival teaching

provenance.note: Atlas entry: used by an estimated few hundred; revival teaching underway
Devised ~1917 by Mohamed Turay; Unicode 7.0 (2014); block U+1E800-1E8DF

scripts.name: Meroitic (Hieroglyphic)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Script of the Kingdom of Kush, in use c. 300 BCE to 400 CE; died out with the Meroitic language and the fall of the Kushite kingdom

provenance.note: Used c. 300 BCE-400 CE; extinct with Meroitic language; ISO 15924 Mero (hieroglyphic) / Merc (cursive); hieroglyphic block U+10980-1099F
ScriptSource Meroitic Hieroglyphs record

scripts.name: Modi (Moḍī)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Used for Marathi 17th c. to 1950s; considered by many to be extinct after replacement by Devanagari, but the subject of active preservation and revival efforts

provenance.note: Used until 1950s; considered by many extinct; revival movement underway; Unicode 7.0; ISO 15924 Modi (324)
ScriptSource Modi record

scripts.name: Mro (Mru)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Mru language classified Definitely Endangered by UNESCO (2010); perhaps as few as 50 Mro can still read and write the script

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Mro/Mru
Created 1980s by Menlay Murang; Mru Definitely Endangered (UNESCO 2010); Unicode block Mro U+16A40-16A6F

scripts.name: N'Ko
scripts.region: West Africa (Guinea, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire and across the Manding region)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Devised 1949 by Solomana Kanté; a grassroots literacy movement has blossomed across West Africa and its standardized use is reported to be growing

provenance.note: Atlas entry for N'Ko
Devised 1949 by Solomana Kanté; RTL; growing usage; Unicode 5.0 (2006); block U+07C0-07FF

scripts.name: Nüshu
scripts.vitalityBasis: The only writing system created and used exclusively by women; last native writer Yang Huanyi died 2004, but undergoing scholarly and grassroots revival

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Nüshu women's script
Last native writer Yang Huanyi died 2004; 396 glyphs added in Unicode 10.0 (June 2017)

scripts.name: Old Permic (Abur)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Devised in the 14th century by Saint Stephen of Perm to write Old Komi; fell out of use by around the 17th century, replaced by Cyrillic

provenance.note: Created 14th c. by Stephen of Perm; obsolete by ~17th c.; ISO 15924 Perm (227); block U+10350-1037F
ScriptSource Old Permic record

scripts.name: 'Phags-pa
scripts.region: Mongol Yuan-dynasty empire (East and Central Asia)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Designed 1269 by Drogön Chögyal Phagpa as a universal script for the Mongol Empire; fell out of use after the fall of the Yuan dynasty

provenance.note: Designed 1269; Tibetan-derived; obsolete after Yuan dynasty; ISO 15924 Phag (331); block U+A840-A87F
ScriptSource 'Phags-pa record

scripts.name: Rejang (Surat Ulu)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Brahmic abugida of the Rejang people of Sumatra; a traditional indigenous script with very limited contemporary everyday use

provenance.note: Brahmic abugida of Sumatra; ISO 15924 Rjng (363); block U+A930-A95F
ScriptSource Rejang record

scripts.name: Sharada (Śāradā)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Once the principal script of Kashmir; now rarely used except by the Kashmiri Pandit community for religious purposes, displaced by Perso-Arabic script in the 1950s

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Sharada
Evolved from Gupta Brahmi 9th c.; now rarely used except by Kashmiri Pandits for religious purposes; ISO 15924 Shrd (319)

scripts.name: Siddham (Siddhaṃ)
scripts.region: India, with liturgical use in East Asian Buddhism (Japan, China)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Historic Brahmic script for Sanskrit; superseded in India but preserved in East Asian (esp. Japanese Shingon) Buddhist liturgical and calligraphic use

provenance.note: Brahmic Sanskrit script; preserved in East Asian Buddhism; ISO 15924 Sidd (302); block U+11580-115FF
ScriptSource Siddham record

scripts.name: Sora Sompeng (Sorang Sompeng)
scripts.family: Brahmic-influenced (created script for a Munda language)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Created 1936 by Mangei Gomango for the Sora (Munda) language (~310,000 speakers); minority/indigenous script documented in the Atlas of Endangered Alphabets

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Sorang Sompeng
ScriptSource Sora record; encoded in Unicode 6.1

scripts.name: Soyombo
scripts.vitalityBasis: Abugida invented by Zanabazar in 1686 for Mongolian/Tibetan/Sanskrit; no longer in everyday use, survives chiefly through the Soyombo national symbol

provenance.note: Invented 1686 by Zanabazar; encoded in Unicode 10.0; ISO 15924 Soyo (329)
ScriptSource record for Soyombo

scripts.name: Tagbanwa
scripts.vitalityBasis: Philippine Brahmic script of the Tagbanwa people; usage has declined sharply and it is now known to relatively few community members

provenance.note: Philippine Brahmic abugida; declining use; ISO 15924 Tagb (373); block U+1760-177F
ScriptSource Tagbanwa record

scripts.name: Tangut
scripts.vitalityBasis: Writes the extinct Tangut (Tibeto-Burman) language; widely used 1036-1502, fell into obscurity after the language's extinction

provenance.note: Used 1036-1502; language extinct; encoded Unicode 9.0; ISO 15924 Tang (520)
ScriptSource Tangut record

scripts.name: Tifinagh (Neo-Tifinagh)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Neo-Tifinagh standardized by IRCAM and made the official script for Tamazight in Morocco since 2003; a revival symbol of Amazigh identity, though everyday adoption remains limited

provenance.note: Neo-Tifinagh official for Tamazight in Morocco since 2003; LTR; Unicode block U+2D30-2D7F
Tifinagh and Berber languages overview

scripts.name: Tolong Siki
scripts.vitalityBasis: Alphabet created 1999 by Narayan Oraon for the Kurukh (Dravidian) language; minority script with non-universal acceptance, documented in the Atlas of Endangered Alphabets

provenance.note: Atlas entry for Tolong Siki
Created 1999 by Narayan Oraon for Kurukh; added in Unicode 17.0 (2025), block U+11DB0-11DEF; ISO 15924 Tols

scripts.name: Vai
scripts.vitalityBasis: Indigenous non-colonial syllabary created in the 1830s; documented in the Atlas of Endangered Alphabets among scripts at risk, though comparatively well-established

provenance.note: Atlas entry: indigenous non-colonial script; ~104,000 Vai speakers in Liberia
Added to Unicode in 2008; Vai block U+A500-A63F; ISO 15924 Vaii

scripts.name: Warang Citi (Varang Kshiti)
scripts.vitalityBasis: Invented by Lako Bodra for the Ho (Munda) language; remains a minority script even among the Ho, many of whom write in Devanagari instead

provenance.note: Atlas entry: minority script even among the Ho
Invented by Lako Bodra; Unicode 7.0 (2014); ISO 15924 Wara (262)
